note.explanation: This unit covers how computers represent text, integers, floating-point numbers, and images. It also practises binary arithmetic and signed 4-bit calculations.
examples: Unsigned 2-byte integers use 16 bits, so their range is 0 to 2¹⁶ − 1, or 0 to 65,535.
In 4-bit two's complement, −5 is made by writing 5 as 0101, inverting the bits to 1010, then adding 1 to get 1011.
note.simple: A computer stores information as bits: 0s and 1s. Different rules let those bits represent letters, numbers, and pictures.
note.checkQuestion: What is the range of an unsigned 2-byte integer?
note.title: How computers represent information
steps: For an unsigned integer with n bits, use the range 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.
For a signed 4-bit value, use two's complement: invert the positive number's bits and add 1 to represent its negative.
For binary addition and subtraction, line up the bits and work from right to left, carrying or borrowing as needed.
Unicode assigns code points to characters from many languages.
An image is made of pixels, and RGB represents colour using red, green, and blue.

mcqs.stem: Q2.1. What does ASCII stand for?
rationales: This is the full form of ASCII.
This changes the first word of the correct full form.
This incorrectly uses “Communication” instead of “Code.”
This changes both “American” and “Code” in the full form.

mcqs.stem: Q2.2. Which of the following numbers is a valid binary number?
rationales: The digit 2 is not allowed in a binary number.
A binary number can use only the digits 0 and 1, and this option does.
This option has a decimal point, so it is not a whole binary number as asked here.
The letter A is not a binary digit.

mcqs.stem: Q2.3. How many bits are used in the standard ASCII encoding?
rationales: Standard ASCII uses 7 bits.
Eight bits may be used in extended forms, but standard ASCII uses 7 bits.
Sixteen bits is not the standard ASCII encoding size.
Thirty-two bits is not the standard ASCII encoding size.

options: It uses fewer bits per character
It can represent characters from many different languages
It is backward compatible with binary
It is specific to the English language
mcqs.stem: Q2.4. Which of the following is a key advantage of Unicode over ASCII?
rationales: Unicode's key advantage is its wide character coverage, not using fewer bits.
Unicode can represent characters from many languages and writing systems.
Binary is a way of representing data, not a character set that Unicode is backward compatible with.
Unicode is not specific to English; it supports many languages.

mcqs.stem: Q2.5. How many bytes are used to store a typical integer?
rationales: One byte is not the typical integer size asked for here.
Two bytes may be used for some integers, but the typical size in this question is 4 bytes.
A typical integer is stored using 4 bytes.
Eight bytes is commonly used for larger integer types, not the typical integer here.

options: Signed integers have a larger range
Unsigned integers are stored in floating-point format
Signed integers are only used for positive numbers
mcqs.stem: Q2.6. What is the primary difference between signed and unsigned integers?
rationales: Unsigned integers represent zero and positive values, but not negative values.
This is not the primary difference; for the same number of bits, signed integers include negative values.
Unsigned integers are integer values, not floating-point values.
Signed integers can represent both positive and negative numbers.

mcqs.stem: Q2.7. In the single precision, how many bits are used for the exponent?
rationales: Single precision uses 23 bits for the fraction, not the exponent.
Single precision uses 8 bits for the exponent.
Eleven exponent bits are used in double precision, not single precision.
Fifty-two bits are used for the fraction in double precision.

mcqs.stem: Q2.8. What is the approximate range of values for single-precision floating-point numbers?
rationales: This is the approximate range given for single precision.
These exponents do not give the approximate single-precision range.
This is approximately the range for double precision, not single precision.
These limits are not the approximate single-precision range.

mcqs.stem: Q2.9. What are the tiny dots that make up an image called?
rationales: The tiny dots that make up a digital image are called pixels.
Bits are units of binary data, not the dots in an image.
Bytes are groups of bits, not the dots in an image.
Nodes are not the name for image dots.

mcqs.stem: Q2.10. In an RGB color model, what does RGB stand for?
rationales: RGB stands for Red, Green, Blue.
The second and third words are not the RGB colour components.
The first word is not “Right”; it is “Red.”
The third word is not “Brown”; it is “Blue.”

written.text: Q2.1. What is the primary purpose of the ASCII encoding scheme?
written.finalAnswer: ASCII represents text characters using binary codes.

rubric.why: The answer must identify what ASCII encodes.
rubric.description: States that ASCII represents or encodes characters.
rubric.how: Mention characters or text symbols.

rubric.why: The answer must explain how the characters are represented.
rubric.description: States that characters are represented by binary codes.
rubric.how: Include binary codes or 0s and 1s.

modelAnswer: ASCII assigns binary codes to characters such as letters, digits, and symbols.
Its purpose is to let computers store and process text.

written.text: Q2.2. Explain the difference between ASCII and Unicode.
written.finalAnswer: ASCII encodes a limited set of characters, mainly for English; Unicode can represent characters from many languages and writing systems.

rubric.why: The comparison must describe ASCII's more limited character set.
rubric.description: Says ASCII represents a limited set of characters, mainly English.
rubric.how: Identify ASCII as limited or mainly English.

rubric.why: The comparison must state Unicode's wider character coverage.
rubric.description: Says Unicode supports characters from many languages.
rubric.how: Mention Unicode and its broad language coverage.

modelAnswer: ASCII encodes a limited set of characters, mainly for English.
Unicode can represent characters from many different languages and writing systems.

written.text: Q2.3. How does Unicode handle characters from different languages?
written.finalAnswer: Unicode assigns a unique code point to each character, allowing characters from many languages to be represented.

rubric.why: A code point is the key way Unicode identifies a character.
rubric.description: Explains that Unicode assigns code points to characters.
rubric.how: State that each character is given a code point.

rubric.why: The answer must connect Unicode's system to different languages.
rubric.description: States that this allows characters from many languages to be represented.
rubric.how: Mention its broad language coverage.

modelAnswer: Unicode assigns a unique code point to each character.
This allows characters from many languages and writing systems to be represented.

written.text: Q2.4. What is the range of values for an unsigned 2-byte integer?

rubric.why: The range depends on the number of bits available.
rubric.description: Identifies that 2 bytes contain 16 bits.
rubric.how: Convert 2 bytes to 16 bits.

rubric.why: The final range must include both correct endpoints.
rubric.description: Gives the range from 0 to 65,535.
rubric.how: Use 0 to 2¹⁶ − 1.

modelAnswer: 2 bytes = 16 bits.
For an unsigned integer, the range is 0 to 2¹⁶ − 1.
The range is 0 to 65,535.

written.text: Q2.5. Explain how a negative integer is represented in binary.
written.finalAnswer: A negative integer is commonly represented using two's complement: invert the bits of its positive value and add 1.

rubric.why: The answer must name the signed representation method.
rubric.description: Identifies two's complement as the method.
rubric.how: Write or name two's complement.

rubric.why: The process requires complementing the bits and adding one.
rubric.description: Explains that the bits are inverted and 1 is added.
rubric.how: Include both operations in the correct order.

modelAnswer: Write the positive integer in binary using the required number of bits.
Invert all the bits.
Add 1 to obtain the two's complement representation of the negative integer.

written.text: Q2.6. What is the benefit of using unsigned integers?
written.finalAnswer: Unsigned integers use all their bits to represent zero and positive values, giving a larger positive range than signed integers of the same size.

rubric.why: Unsigned integers represent non-negative quantities.
rubric.description: States that unsigned integers represent zero and positive values.
rubric.how: Mention non-negative values.

rubric.why: The benefit is a wider non-negative range for the same bit count.
rubric.description: States that unsigned integers can represent a larger positive range than signed integers of the same size.
rubric.how: Compare the positive range for the same number of bits.

modelAnswer: Unsigned integers do not need to represent negative values.
Therefore, all their bits are used for zero and positive values, giving a larger positive range than a signed integer of the same size.

written.text: Q2.7. How does the number of bits affect the range of integer values?
written.finalAnswer: More bits allow more values to be represented; an unsigned n-bit integer ranges from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.

rubric.why: The answer must state the relationship between bits and the number of possible values.
rubric.description: Explains that increasing the number of bits increases the number of representable values.
rubric.how: State that more bits give a wider range.

rubric.why: The formula demonstrates how the range depends on the bit count.
rubric.description: Gives the unsigned range as 0 to 2ⁿ − 1, or an equivalent correct explanation.
rubric.how: Use the n-bit range formula.

modelAnswer: Each additional bit doubles the number of possible bit patterns.
For an unsigned n-bit integer, the range is 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.

written.text: Q2.8. Why are whole numbers commonly used in computing for quantities that cannot be negative?
written.finalAnswer: Unsigned whole numbers are suitable because they represent zero and positive values without using any values for negatives.

rubric.why: The answer must connect the choice to the quantity's possible values.
rubric.description: Recognises that the quantities are zero or positive.
rubric.how: State that the quantities cannot be negative.

rubric.why: Unsigned representation makes the available range useful for these quantities.
rubric.description: Explains that unsigned whole numbers represent non-negative quantities efficiently.
rubric.how: Mention unsigned integers or their non-negative range.

modelAnswer: These quantities are zero or positive and cannot be negative.
Unsigned whole numbers are suitable because they represent non-negative values and use their bits for that range.

written.text: Q2.9. How is the range of floating-point numbers calculated for single precision?
written.finalAnswer: Single precision uses 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 23 fraction bits; its approximate range is 1.4 x 10⁻⁴⁵ to 3.4 x 10³⁸.

rubric.why: The exponent bits determine the scale and range of floating-point values.
rubric.description: Identifies the 8-bit exponent in single precision.
rubric.how: State that single precision has 8 exponent bits.

rubric.why: The approximate range is the numerical result being asked for.
rubric.description: Gives the approximate range 1.4 x 10⁻⁴⁵ to 3.4 x 10³⁸.
rubric.how: Include the approximate minimum and maximum.

modelAnswer: Single precision has 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 23 fraction bits.
The exponent bits set the scale of the values that can be represented.
Its approximate range is 1.4 x 10⁻⁴⁵ to 3.4 x 10³⁸.

written.text: Q2.10. Why is it important to understand the limitations of floating-point representation in scientific computing?
written.finalAnswer: Floating-point numbers have limited precision and range, so rounding errors and overflow or underflow can affect scientific calculations.

rubric.why: Limited precision can make stored values differ slightly from exact values.
rubric.description: Mentions limited precision or rounding error.
rubric.how: Explain that a value may be rounded or approximated.

rubric.why: Values outside the representable range can also affect calculations.
rubric.description: Mentions overflow, underflow, or another consequence of limited range.
rubric.how: Connect the representation limits to possible calculation errors.

modelAnswer: Floating-point numbers have limited precision, so some values are rounded or stored as approximations.
They also have a limited range, so overflow or underflow can occur and affect scientific results.

written.text: Q2.1. Explain how characters are encoded using Unicode. Provide examples of characters from different languages and their corresponding Unicode code points.
written.finalAnswer: Unicode assigns code points to characters; for example, A is U+0041, ا is U+0627, and ब is U+092C.

rubric.why: The central idea is that Unicode identifies characters using code points.
rubric.description: Explains that Unicode assigns a code point to each character.
rubric.how: Describe the code point mapping.

rubric.why: Unicode's purpose includes representing characters from many languages.
rubric.description: Explains that Unicode supports different languages and writing systems.
rubric.how: State that its character set is not limited to English.

rubric.why: Correct examples show how code points identify actual characters.
rubric.description: Gives at least two correct character and code point examples.
rubric.how: Use examples from different languages, such as A, ا, and ब.

rubric.why: The final answer must include correctly matched examples.
rubric.description: Correctly matches the examples to their Unicode code points.
rubric.how: Give A as U+0041, ا as U+0627, and ब as U+092C.

modelAnswer: Unicode assigns a unique code point to each character.
The code point identifies the character, while an encoding such as UTF-8 stores it as bytes in a computer.
For example, the English letter A has the code point U+0041.
The Arabic letter ا has the code point U+0627.
The Devanagari letter ब has the code point U+092C.
These examples show how Unicode can represent characters from different languages.

written.text: Q2.2. Describe in detail how integers are stored in computer memory.
written.finalAnswer: Integers are stored as binary bit patterns. Unsigned integers use all bits for non-negative values; signed integers commonly use two's complement to represent positive and negative values.

rubric.why: The answer must establish that memory stores integer values as bit patterns.
rubric.description: Explains that integers are stored using binary bits in memory.
rubric.how: Mention bits or 0s and 1s.

rubric.why: Unsigned storage is an important integer representation.
rubric.description: Explains that unsigned integers represent zero and positive values.
rubric.how: Describe the unsigned range or meaning.

rubric.why: The method for storing signed integers must be identified.
rubric.description: Explains that signed integers use two's complement to represent negatives.
rubric.how: Name two's complement and connect it to negative values.

rubric.why: A correct answer should connect the number of bits with the representable range.
rubric.description: Explains that the bit count determines the range and gives a correct range rule or example.
rubric.how: State that more bits allow more values, or give an appropriate range formula.

modelAnswer: Computer memory stores an integer as a pattern of binary bits, each having a value of 0 or 1.
The number of bits allocated to the integer determines how many different values can be stored.
For an unsigned n-bit integer, all bit patterns represent non-negative values, from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.
A signed integer must also represent negative values.
A common signed representation is two's complement.
To form a negative value in two's complement, write the positive value in binary, invert its bits, and add 1.
For example, in 4 bits, 5 is 0101; invert to get 1010 and add 1 to get 1011, which represents −5.
Thus, the same bit pattern is interpreted according to whether the integer is signed or unsigned.

written.text:
Q2.3. Explain the process of converting a decimal integer to its binary representation and vice versa. Include examples of both positive and
negative integers.

rubric.why: Repeated division by 2 is the standard decimal-to-binary method.
rubric.description: Explains how to convert a positive decimal integer to binary.
rubric.how: Divide repeatedly by 2 and read the remainders from bottom to top.

rubric.why: Binary-to-decimal conversion uses powers of 2 as place values.
rubric.description: Explains how to convert a binary number to decimal.
rubric.how: Multiply each bit by its power of 2 and add.

rubric.why: Negative values in the example must use the two's complement process.
rubric.description: Explains how to represent a negative value using two's complement.
rubric.how: Use a fixed bit width, invert the positive bits, and add 1.

rubric.why: The final answer must demonstrate positive and negative conversions correctly.
rubric.description: Gives correct examples, including a positive decimal-binary pair and a negative two's complement pair.
rubric.how: Include 13₁₀ = 1101₂ and, in 4 bits, −5₁₀ = 1011₂.

modelAnswer: To convert a positive decimal integer to binary, divide by 2 repeatedly and record each remainder.
Read the remainders from bottom to top.
For 13: 13 ÷ 2 = 6 remainder 1; 6 ÷ 2 = 3 remainder 0; 3 ÷ 2 = 1 remainder 1; 1 ÷ 2 = 0 remainder 1.
Therefore, 13₁₀ = 1101₂.
To convert binary to decimal, multiply each bit by its power-of-2 place value and add: 1101₂ = 1 × 8 + 1 × 4 + 0 × 2 + 1 × 1 = 13₁₀.
For a negative integer, use a fixed number of bits and two's complement.
In 4 bits, 5 is 0101; invert the bits to get 1010 and add 1 to get 1011.
Therefore, −5₁₀ = 1011₂ in 4-bit two's complement; conversely, 1011₂ represents −5₁₀.

written.text: Q2.4. Perform the following binary arithmetic operations:  (a) Multiplication of 101₂ by 11₂.  (b) Division of 1100₂ by 10₂.

rubric.why: Correct partial products are needed for the multiplication.
rubric.description: Sets up or shows correct binary multiplication.
rubric.how: Multiply by each bit of 11₂ and shift the second partial product.

rubric.why: The multiplication must end with the correct binary product.
rubric.description: Gives 101₂ × 11₂ = 1111₂.
rubric.how: Add the partial products correctly.

rubric.why: The division working must use the correct dividend and divisor.
rubric.description: Shows division of 1100₂ by 10₂.
rubric.how: Divide by 10₂, which shifts the binary number one place right.

rubric.why: The final quotient must be correct.
rubric.description: Gives 1100₂ ÷ 10₂ = 110₂.
rubric.how: State the correct quotient.

modelAnswer: 101₂ × 1₂, shifted one place left = 1010₂
Therefore, 101₂ × 11₂ = 1111₂.
Therefore, 1100₂ ÷ 10₂ = 110₂.

written.text: Q2.6. Add the following binary numbers:  (a)  101₂ + 110₂  (b)  1100₂ + 1011₂

rubric.why: Correct alignment is needed before adding binary columns.
rubric.description: Lines up the numbers correctly for part (a).
rubric.how: Place the rightmost bits in the same column.

rubric.why: The sum for part (a) must be correct.
rubric.how: Carry correctly when a column adds to 2 or 3.

rubric.why: Correct alignment and carrying are required for part (b).
rubric.description: Shows the addition of 1100₂ and 1011₂.
rubric.how: Add from right to left and carry when needed.

rubric.why: The final result for part (b) must be correct.
rubric.how: Write the correct final sum.

modelAnswer: Therefore, 101₂ + 110₂ = 1011₂.
Therefore, 1100₂ + 1011₂ = 10111₂.

written.text: Q2.7. Convert the following numbers to 4-bit binary and add them:  (a) 7 + (-4)  (b) -5 + 3

rubric.why: Both numbers must be represented correctly in 4-bit two's complement.
rubric.description: Converts 7 and −4 to 4-bit binary.
rubric.how: Use 0111 for 7 and form −4 by two's complement.

rubric.why: The first 4-bit addition must give the correct result.
rubric.description: Adds the 4-bit representations for part (a).
rubric.how: Add the bits and give 0011₂.

rubric.why: Both numbers in part (b) must be represented correctly.
rubric.description: Converts −5 and 3 to 4-bit two's complement.
rubric.how: Use 1011 for −5 and 0011 for 3.

rubric.why: The second addition must give the correct 4-bit answer.
rubric.description: Adds the representations for part (b) and gives 1110₂.
rubric.how: Add the bits and state the 4-bit result.

modelAnswer: (a) In 4 bits, 7 = 0111₂.
To represent −4: 4 = 0100₂; invert to get 1011₂; add 1 to get 1100₂.
Therefore, 7 + (−4) = 0011₂.
(b) In 4 bits, 5 = 0101₂; invert to get 1010₂; add 1 to get 1011₂, so −5 = 1011₂.
In 4 bits, 3 = 0011₂.
Therefore, −5 + 3 = 1110₂.

rubric.why: Correct place alignment and borrowing are needed for subtraction.
rubric.description: Shows suitable working for part (a).
rubric.how: Align bits by place value and subtract from right to left.

rubric.why: The first two binary differences must be correct.
rubric.description: Gives the correct answers to parts (a) and (b).
rubric.how: Write 1001₂ and 0111₂.

rubric.why: Correct subtraction working is required for parts (c) and (d).
rubric.description: Shows suitable working for the remaining subtractions.
rubric.how: Align the bits and borrow correctly where needed.

rubric.why: The final two results must be correct.
rubric.description: Gives the correct answers to parts (c) and (d).
rubric.how: Write 0010₂ and 1010₂.

modelAnswer: (d) Write 100₂ as 0100₂ to align the places.

examTips: Section A tests quick facts and definitions, such as ASCII, Unicode, bit counts, pixels, RGB, and integer ranges. Learn the key facts carefully.
Short questions usually earn marks for a correct definition or fact and a brief explanation, formula, or example.
Long questions can ask for an explanation, conversions, or binary arithmetic. Show each step, not just the final result.
For unsigned integers, show the number of bits and use 0 to 2ⁿ − 1. For negative values, state the bit width and show the two's complement steps.
In binary addition and subtraction, line up the numbers, show carries or borrowing where needed, and write the final answer in binary.

yourTurn.question: Q2.6. Add the following binary numbers:  (a)  101₂ + 110₂
solution: In the left column, 1 + 1 = 10₂; write 0 and carry 1.
Write the carried 1 in the next column.

steps.why: Use the same number of bits for both numbers so the 4-bit addition is clear.
For a negative value, first write the positive value in 4-bit binary.
Inverting every bit begins the two's complement process.
Adding 1 completes the two's complement representation of −4.
The numbers are now in the required 4-bit form and can be added column by column.
The carries are handled in the binary addition, leaving the 4-bit sum shown.
The sum is positive 3, written as 0011 in 4-bit binary.

explain.title: Characters and codes
explain.body: ASCII gives binary codes to a limited set of text characters. Unicode gives code points to characters from many languages and writing systems.

explain.title: Integers in memory
explain.body: Integers are stored as bits. Unsigned integers represent zero and positive values; signed integers can represent negative values, commonly using two's complement.

explain.title: Bit count and number range
explain.body: More bits allow more possible values. An unsigned integer with n bits ranges from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.

explain.title: Floating-point numbers
explain.body: Single precision uses 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 23 fraction bits. It represents a wide range of values, but its precision and range are limited.

explain.title: Binary arithmetic and images
explain.body: Binary numbers can be added, subtracted, multiplied, and divided using place values and carries. Images are made of pixels; RGB means Red, Green, Blue.

mistakes: Using the digit 2 or another non-binary digit in a binary number.
Forgetting that 2 bytes contain 16 bits, or using the signed range for an unsigned integer.
Finding a negative two's complement value by inverting the bits but forgetting to add 1.
Not keeping the required bit width when adding signed 4-bit numbers.
Adding binary columns without carrying, or subtracting without aligning the place values.
Confusing single-precision exponent bits with fraction bits: the exponent has 8 bits and the fraction has 23 bits.
